Mounting Arrears to Central PSUs from SEBs 
399. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether Government have evolved a scheme to deal with the 
mounting arrears of payments due to Central PSUs from the State Electricity 
Boards; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the progress made in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Under the Chairmanship of 
the Prime Minister a Chief Ministers' Conference was held in March, 2001. 
Among other issues the Conference resolv ed to constitute an Expert Group 
to recommend a one time settlement of outstanding dues of the SEBs to the 
CPSUs and dues from the CPSUs to the State Power Utilities. 
An Expert Group under the Chairmanship of Shri M.S. Ahluwalia, the 
then Member (Energy), Planning Commission was constituted in March, 2001. 
The Expert Group has since submitted two reports. The first report relating to 
one time settlement of outstanding dues was submitted in May, 2001 and the 
second report relating to capital rest ructuring and reforms was submitted in 
July, 2001. 
The main features of the scheme recommended by the Expert Group for 
one time settlement of outstanding dues are as under:— 
(a) The Group recommended 50 per cent waiver of surcharge/ interest on 
delayed payments. 
(b) For the remaining dues i.e. the entire principal outstanding as well as 
the remaining 50% surcharge, bonds would be issued by the respective State 
Governments. 
(c) The bonds would be issued through RBI at a tax free interest rate of 
8.5% p.a. 
128 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The bonds should be structured to achieve a moratorium of 5 years on 
repayment of principal with the entire principal being repaid between 
the 6th and 15th year. 
(e) These bonds shall be identical to bonds issued in connection with the 
market borrowings of State Governments, with the attendant discipline 
in repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock-in restrictions that 
will allow release of only 10 per cent of the bonds in the secondary 
market each year. 
(f) For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel shou ld attract a graded reduction in 
the supply of power from central power stations and in coal supplies. 
Where such defaults exceed 90 days from the date of billing, the 
Ministry of Finance should recover these dues through adjustment 
against releases dues to them from the Centre. 
(g) As part of the scheme, SEBs should accept reform-based performance 
milestones such as setting up of SERCs, metering of distribution 
feeders and improvement in revenue realisation. The milestones should 
be specified in the MOUs to be signed with the Ministry of Power. 
(h) The State should be offered incentives for complying with the scheme. 
If SEBs do not default on their current dues and adhere to the 
performance milestones, CPSUs should pay them, during the first four 
years commencing from 1.4.2001, bi-annual cash incentives equal to 2 
per cent of the value of bonds. 
(i) Further— if SEBs open and maintain LCs till the end of December, 
2001, CPSUs should pay them a one-time cash incentive equal to 2 per 
cent of the value of bonds. 
(j) In addition, States undertaking reforms should also be assisted through 
APDP grants and discretionary allocation of power. 
(k) This scheme should enter into force only after one-half of the States 
that have an annual billing of over Rs. 500 crore per annum from 
CPSUs give their consent, and should be effective in respect of the 
States that give such consent. 
(l) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2001] 
scheme enters into force should be denied any share in the 
discretionary allocation of 15 per cent from the power stations of 
CPSUs as well as any assistance unde r APDP. If the overdues of such 
States exceeded Rs. 50 crores in respect of any CPSU, they should also 
attract reduction in power and coal supplies, as applicable to the States 
participating in this scheme. 
Following the submission of the Report of the Expert Group a high level 
Empowered Group consisting of Finance Minister, Dy. Chairman, Planning 
Commission, Minister of Power and Chief Ministers of some States met on 
26.6.2001 and 6.7.2001. The Empowered Group endorsed the 
recommendations of the Expert Group with the following modifications:— 
(i) Waiver of surcharge would now be 60% instead of 50% as 
recommended by the Group. 
(ii) The incentives for achieving the reform-based milestones shall be 
increased to 6% in the first year and 5% in the second year. 
Recently, Minister of Power has written to Chief Ministers of States and 
UTs urging them to initiate necessary steps for implementation of the scheme 
at the earliest.

Allocation of power from Central Power Corporations 
401. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  the present formula adopted by 
Government for allocation of power from the power stations of Central 
Power Corporations viz. NTPC, NHPC, NPC etc. needs review; 
(b) whether Rajasthan Government has expressed that the present formula 
is not based on the analogy of distribution of Central taxes/ plan assistance to 
the States etc. resulting in lesser allo cation to the States from the Central 
sector power stations as a result States given higher allocation are selling 
power to Rajasthan; and 
(c) if so, whether Centre will review the above formula? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) According to the formula 
for sharing of power from Central Sector power stations, power was allocated 
among the States/UTs of a region in accordance 
132 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
with the Central Plan Assistance and act ual energy consumption in the State 
of the region for previous five years, the two factors being given equal 
weightage. The Gadgil formula which forms the basis of Central Plan 
Assistance to the States, in its different modified forms, has been giving 
weightage to the population to the extent of 60 to 70%. According to the 
latest modification of the Gadgil formula, weightage to population in the 
Central Plan Assistance is 60%. Since the formula is also based on the actual 
consumption of energy, it indirectly takes care of the surplus power in certain 
States which is sold to deficit States for consumption. 
It has been decided by the Government in April, 2000 to treat the existing 
"Formula" for allocation of power to the StatesUTs from new Central Sector 
power stations as "guidelines" so as to link the allocation of power with their 
need and capacity to pay. However, ther e is no change in the contents of the 
formula and it does not disturb the allocation already made from the Central 
Sector power stations. Under the "guidelines" power from the new Central 
Sector power stations will be made to the States/UTs as per their entitlement 
subject to the Power Purchase Agreements  (PPAs) to be signed by them with 
the CPSUs concerned. No further review of the "guidelines" is presently 
envisaged.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) As per provisions of Section 47(1) 
of the Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000, the assets and liabilities relating to any 
commercial or industrial undertaking of the existing State of Bihar shall pass 
to the State in which the undertaking is located. Jharkhand Government has 
issued a notification dated 27.2.2001 taking over the Tenughat Vidyut Nigam

and Others in the Patna High Court for quashing the notification dated 
27.2.2001 issued by the Government of Jharkhand, whereby Tenughat Vidyut 
Nigam Ltd. was notified as an undertaking of the State of Jharkhand. 
However, the High Court in its judgement dated 27.6.2001 has dismissed the 
PIL. 
(b) and (c) For apportionment of assets and liabilities to make the new 
Jharkhand State Electricity Board functional, Central Government in exercise 
of the powers conferred upon it by clause (a) of sub section (4) of Section 62 
of the Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000 has notified order on 22nd March, 2001 
for provisional allocation of assets, liabilities, rights and undertaking of the 
existing Board between Boards of Bihar and Jharkhand with effect from 
1.4.2001.

 SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA':

power by producers to consumers directly but only through the SEBs and if

408. SHRI BRAHMAKUMAR BHATT: Will the Minister of POWER be

(b) if so, the details thereof;

(f) whether the above bids were treated as non-responsive and decided to 
rebid; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (g) The Government of Gujarat have 
recommended the following power projects to the Centra! Electricity Authority 
(CEA) for Techno-Economic Clearance (TEC). 
(1) 106.617 MW Gas based Power Plant at Dhuvran by Gujarat State 
Electricity Corporation Limited. 
(2) Hazira Combined Cycle Power Proj ect (156 MW) by Gujarat State 
Energy Generation Limited. 
TEC in respect of Hazira Combined Cycle Power Project has been accorded by 
CEA in September, 2000. In respect of Dhuvran Project, 
148 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
the Detailed Project Report was received in CEA on 30.3.2000. The TEC for 
the project was held up due to non-availability of important 
inputs/clearances, and subsequent changes in EPC contract. 
In addition to above projects, the National, Thermal Power Corporation 
Limited (NTPC) had planned expansion of Ka was, Jhanor-Gandhar gas 
power stations by addi ng 650 MW generating capacity at each of these 
stations. As additional gas linkage wa s not available, expansion of these 
projects was planned with Naphtha as a bridge fuel with provision to switch 
over to LNG, as and when it bacame available. TEC from CEA was obtained 
in August, 1998 and November, 1998 for Kawas and Jhanor-Gandhar 
projects respectively. The bids for main plant package for Kawas were 
invited in September, 1998 and the bids for main plant package for Jhanor-
Gandhar clubbed with Kawas were invited in November, 1998. The bids for 
these projects were opended on 30-6-1999. Two bids were received: one from 
BHEL and other from ABB. Since the bids received were non-responsive, 
NTPC decided to go for rebidding. 
However, in view of the abnormal increase in Naphtha prices in the recent 
past, NTPC has decided to match commissioning of these projects with the 
availability of imported regasified LNG at a reasonable price. In view of the 
estimated cost of generation at about Rs. 4 per unit, NTPC had sought 
reconfirmation from beneficiaries fo r availing power from these expansion 
projects at this indicative price to enable NTPC to take up construction of 
these projects. A number of beneficiar ies have expressed their unwillingness 
to purchase power at this high cost of generation. NTPC will, therefore, take 
up further processing of these expansion proposals and further action towards 
bidding for main equipment only after confirmation of LNG at a reasonable 
firm price and acceptance of the cost of generation based OR LNG price by 
the beneficiaries.

Recommendations of Expert Group Headed By Shri M.S. Ahluwalia 
410. SHRI C. RAMAC HANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have by now received the 
recommendations of the high level expert group headed by the 
former Planning Commission member Shri M.S. Ahluwalia to suggest 
measures for settlement of outstanding dues of State Electricity 
Boards to Central utilities like NTPC, Railways, etc. and future 
strategy for their capital restructuring; 
(b) if so, details of main recommedations; 
(c) the reaction of Union Government thereto; 
150 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether State Governments have favourably- reacted to these 
recommendations; and 
(e) if so, details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) Under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister a Chief Minister's 
Conference was held in March, 2001. Among other issues the Conference 
resolved to constitute and Expert Group to recommended a one time 
settlement of outstanding dues of the SEBs to the CPSU and dues from the 
CPSU to the State Power Utilities. 
An Expert Group under the Chairmanship of Shri M.S. Ahluwalia, the then 
Member (Energy), Planning Commission was constituted in March, 2001. The 
Expert Group has since submitted two reports. The first report relating to one 
time settlement of outstanding dues was submitted in May, 2001 and the 
second report relating to capital restructuring and reforms was submitted in 
July, 2001. 
The main features of the scheme recommended by the Expert Group for 
one time settlement of outstanding dues are as under:— 
(a) The Group recommended 50 per cent waiver of surcharge/ interest on 
delayed payments. 
(b) For the remaining dues i.e. the entire principal outstanding as well as 
the remaining 50% surcharge, bonds would be issued by the respective State 
Governments. 
(c) The bonds would be issued through RBI at a tax free interest rate 
8.5% p.a. 
 
(d) The bonds should struct ured to achieve a moratorium of 5 years on 
repayment of principal with the entire principal being repaid between the 6th 
and 15th year. 
(e) These bonds shall be identical to bonds issued in connection with   the   
market   borrowing   of   State   Governments,   with   the 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2001] 
attendant discipline in repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock-in 
restrictions that will allow release of only 10 per cent of the bonds in the 
secondary market each year. 
(f) For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults 
in current payment for powerful/fuel should attract a graded 
reduction in the supply of power from central power stations and in 
coal supplies. Where such defaults exceed 90 days from the date of 
billing, the Ministry of Finance should recover these dues through 
adjustment against release dues to them from the Centre. 
(g) As part of the scheme, SEB should accept reform-based 
performance milestones such as setting up SERCs, metering of 
distribution feeders and improvement in revenue realisation. The 
milestones should be specified in the MoUs to be signed with the 
Ministry of Power. 
(h) The State should be offered incentives for complying with the scheme. 
If SEBs do not default on their current dues and adhere to the performance 
milestones, CPSUs should pay them, dur ing the first four year commencing 
from 1.4.2001, biannual cash incentives equal to 2 per cent of the value of 
bonds. 
(i) Further, if SEBs open and mainta in LCs till the end of December 2001, 
CPSUs should pay them a one-time cash incentive equal to 2 per cent of the 
value of bonds. 
(j) In addition, State un dertaking reforms should al so be asssisted through 
APDP grants and discretionary allocation of power. 
(k) This scheme should enter into force only after one-half of the States 
that have an annual billing of over Rs. 500 crore per annum from CPSUs give 
their consent, and should be effective in  respect of the State that give such 
consent. 
(1) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this scheme 
enters into force should be denied any share in the discretionary allocation of 
15 per cent from the power stations of CPSUs as well as any assistance under 
APDP. If the overdues of such States  exceeded  Rs.   50  crores  in  respect  
of any  CPSU,  they 
152 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
should   also   attract   reduction   in   power   and   coal   supplies,   as applicable 
to the State participating in this scheme. 
Following the submission of the Report of the Expert Group a high level 
Empowered Group consisting of Finance Minister, Dy. Chairman, Planning 
Commission, Minister of Power and Chief Ministers of some States met on 
26.6.2001 and 6.7.2001. The Empowered Group endorsed the 
recommendations of the Expert Group with the following modifications:— 
(i) Waiver of surcharge would now be 60% instead of 50% as recommended 
by the Group. 
(ii) The incentives for achieving th e reform based milestones shall be 
increased to 6% in the first year 5% in the second year. 
Recently, Minister of Power has written to Chief Ministers of States and 
UTs urging them to initiate necessary steps for implementation of the scheme 
at the earliest. 
The second report of the Expert Group has also been received recently and 
is under examination.

Renovation of Galibaha Power Station, Sultanpur (UP) 
† 413. SHRI SURYABHAN PATIL VAHADANE: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that Galiobaha power 
station, Sultanpur (Uttar Pradesh), wh ich was installed to provide power 
supply in rural areas, has totally failed to fulfil its objective; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government are also aware of the fact that lakhs of rupees are 
spent annually in the name of renovation of machines of the said station 
whereas renovation work actually never takes place; and 
(d) the details of amount spent by the power station on the 
renovation work in the last three years and work actually completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) to (d) According to information 
furnished by Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd., Galibaha power station, 
Sultanpur has not filed to meet its obj ective to provide power supply to rural 
areas. Requisite renovation works, duly approved have been completed and 
the sanctioned expenditure was incurred. 
During the last three years, the following renovation works have been 
completed with the estimated cost of Rs. 15.22 lakhs: 
1. Damaged incoming 11 kV OCB replaced with the new one on 20.9.1999 
with the estimated cost of Rs. 1.79 lakhs, which includes cost of new 
machineries as well. 
2. Damaged feeders of 11 kV OCB repl aced with new one in September, 
1999 with the estimated cost of Rs. 2.03 lakhs. 
3. 3341 kV, 3 MVA Power transformer upgraded to 5 MVA in October, 
1999 with the estimated cost of Rs. 11.40 lakhs.

Rehabilitation of the Tehri Dam oustees 
414. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Mi nister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the progress made so far in rehabilitation of the Tehri Dam oustees 
indicating details of resettlement schemes with regard to urban and rural 
areas submerged, indicating the families uprooted and rehabilitated and land 
for housing and other purposes allotted/ allocated; 
(b) whether the rehabilitation of oustees is behind schedule; and 
(c) the expenditure so far incurred thereon, and the extent of funds-
crunch suffered and the delay caused thereby? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) and (b) The rehabilitation and 
resettlement of persons affected by the construction of Tehri HEP Stage-I 
(1000 MW) is being undertaken in two phases. While Phase-I relates to 
families affected by the construction of Coffer Dam, Phase-II covers the 
families affected by the construction of the Main Dam and the impoundment 
of reservoir. The activities relating to Rehabilitation and Resettlement would 
be completed pari-passu with the co mpletion of Tehri HEP. Details of 
progress of rehabilitation of urban and rural project affected families are 
given in the statement. (See below) 
(c) Against the provision of Rs. 862.57 crores (at August, 1999 price 
level) for rehabilitation relating to Tehri Project Stage-I, an expenditure of 
about Rs. 600 crores has been incurre d so far. There has been no funds 
crunch for rehabilitation works.

Government intervention in Enron 
415. DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Union Government proposed to intervene in Enron issue; 
and 
(b) if so, the reaction of the Maharashtra Government thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA) : (a) and (b) The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) 
for purchase of power supplied by the Dabhol Power project in Maharashtra 
promoted by Enron was signed between the Maharashtra State Electricity Board 
(MSEB) and the Dabhol Power Company (DPC). Government of India (GOI) 
has issued a counter guarantee to the Phase-I of the Dabhol Power Project 
covering some of the energy and capacity payments as well as termination 
payments. Recently, the GoM have constituted a Negotiating Committee 
under the chairmanship of Dr. Madhav Godbole, ex-Home Secretary to the 
Government of India, to renegotiate th e project with DPC and their lenders, 
etc. The Government of India has agreed to facilitate an amicable solution and has 
appointed its nominee on the Negotiating Committee.

National Social Assistance Programme in Himachal Pradesh 
† 417. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: W ill the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the schemes introduced under the National Social Assistance 
        programme in Himachal Pradesh; 
(b) The amount spent on the same during the year 1999-2000 alongwith 
the number of persons benefited by the said programme; 
(c) whether Government have constituted any specific study group in this 
regard; 
(d) if so, the full details thereof alo ngwith the progress made by them; 
and 
(e) district-wise and panchayat-wise details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEV ELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) All the three components of the National Social Assistance 
Programme (NSAP) namely: (i) National Old Age Pension Scheme 
(NOAPS), (ii) National Family Benef it Scheme (NFBS), and (iii) National 
Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS), have  been introduced in the State of 
Himachal Pradesh. The NMBS has, however, been transferred to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare w.e.f. 1.4.2001, and as such, is no 
longer a component of NSAP. 
(b) During the year 1999-2000, the State of Himachal Pradesh was 
released Rs. 233.29 lakh, Rs.29.37 lakh and Rs. 12.22 lakh under NOAPS, 
NFBS and NMBS respectively. The utilisation and the number of 
beneficiaries reported by the State Government are Rs. 191.54 lakh under 
NOAPS (15176 beneficiaries), Rs. 40.27 lakh under NFBS (451 
beneficiaries) and Rs. 17.88 lakh under NMBS (3492 beneficiaries) 
(c) A Quick Evaluation Study of National Social Assistance Programme 
(NSAP) was entrusted to Ms Centre for Management Development,    
Thycaud,    Thiruvanthapuram,    during   2000.    The

the State of Himachal Pradesh.

States according to their performance in the implementation of the NSAP 
Schemes. The ranking scheme was developed by using certain paramenters like 
coverage of the Scheme, utilisation of the funds, economic backwardness of the 
recipients, timeliness of release of benefits, expenditure incurred for the

Food for work Programme In Orissa 
420. SHRI ANANTA SETHI: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the norms prescribed for implementing Food for Work Programme and 
funds spent thereon during 2000-2001 and 2001-2002, so far in Orissa; 
(b) whether the Food for Work Programme is not implemented effectively in 
the State; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps taken to extend the programme to the drought affected areas 
of that State? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) After the Super Cyclone, in Orissa, the F ood For Work 
Programme was started in 14 cyclone affected districts in 1999-2000. The 
funds were shared between Central Government and State Government in the 
ratio of 75:25. The total amount spent on this programme was Rs. 105.00 
crores, out of which an amount of Rs. 78.74 crore was released by the Central 
Government.  Under this programme each labourer was to be 
187 

 
RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2001] 
provided 2kg of rice per day @ Rs. 6.25 per kg. The remaining balance of 
wages amounting of Rs. 27 per day were paid in cash. According to the 
report received from the State Govern ment of Orissa about 22169 MT of 
foodgrain was lifted from FCI gowdowns and distributed. Employment 
generated under this programme was to the tune of 128 lakhs mandays. 
During 2000-2001, a comprehensive Food for Work Programme was 
started in eight notified drought aff ected States including Orissa. The 
norms prescribed for implementation of the scheme are as follows: 
(i) Food For Work Programme will be a general scheme, which can form 
a part of any scheme of the centre and state government being 
implemented for generation of wage employment in the notified 
drought affected districts of the states. 
(ii) The Government of India will make available appropriate quantity of 
foodgrains to each of the affected states as an additionality and free of 
cost with a view to enable the drought affected State to provide 
adequate wage employment opportunities to the needy rural poor. 
(iii) The eligibility criteria for employment has been relaxed so as to 
include both BPL and APL families. 
(iv) The State is free to make payment of wages partly in kind (up to 5 
kgs. of foodgrains per manday) and partly in cash. 
(v) The State Government is free to cal culate the cost of foodgrains paid 
inwages, at either BPL rates or AP L rates or anywhere between these 
two rates. The balance of wages is paid in cash. 
(vi) The cash component of the wages and the material cost is met from 
the scheme under which the Food for Work Programme is 
implemented. 
(vii) The cost of transportation of foodgrains from FCI godowns 
188 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
to the work-site/PDS and its distribution is the responsibility of the 
State Government. 
(b) No, Sir. Under Food For Work Programme, out of 30 
districts, 28 districts of Orissa are covered. During 2000-01, 1,00,000 
tonnes of foodgrains (20,000 tonnes of wheat and 80,000 tonnes of 
rice) was allocated. In the curr ent financial year (2001-02), a 
quantity of 50,000 tonnes of rice for 22 districts, as demanded by 
State Government of Orissa has also been released. According to 
the latest information received so far, the State Government has 
lifted 85,000 tonnes of foodgrains ag ainst allocation of 1,50,000 
tonnes and distributed 77096 tonnes of foodgrains. Employment 
generated is 180 lakhs mandays. 
(c) and (d) Questions  do not arise.

Migration of villagers in search of work in Orissa 
423. SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWD A: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Government of Orissa has admitted that 
people particularly in the drought-hit Western Orissa were leaving their 
villages and migrating to other State in search of work as reproted in New 
Indian Express, Bhubaneswar dated the 21st June, 2001; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the poverty alleviation programmes are not 
properly implemented; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) Yes, sir. The State Govern ment of Orissa has informed that 
many people of the drought affected areas of the districts migrated to 
neighbouring States like Chhattisgarh ahead of the usual migration situation. 
However, the State Government took up extensive drought m itigation 
measures by installing tube-wells, repairing old and defunct tube-wells, 
renovating a very large number of existing water sources and digging up new 
tanks. All habitations 
192 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
were covered with drinking water sources and the problem of drinking water 
could be effectively mitigated. Added to this, extensive labour intensive 
works were taken up by spending funds to the tune of Rs. 76.64 crores from 
the Calamity Relief Fund and by utilising food-grains provided under the 
Food for Work Programme. The State Government of Orissa is of the 
opinion that there was a panic which induced migration for a temporary period 
and not out of distress arising due to drought situation. 
(b) and (c) No Sir. As per the prog ress reports received from the State 
Government of Orissa, during 2000-2001, under EAS and JGSY, 80% and 
86% of funds available were spent respectively on generation of employment 
and creation of rural infrastructure. 
Role of local villagers in community-driven programmes 
424. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that r ecently in one of the meetings of 
the FAO's Committee on World Food Security the role of local villagers in 
community driven programmes was stressed wherein they have started 
experimenting water harvesting, protecting watersheds thereby substantially 
increasing agriculture production and foresty, etc; 
(b) if so, whether the Ministry has launched any such scheme with the 
active involvement of rural population; and 
(c) if so, what are the details of such  schemes and where these have been 
launched? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. .SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) A Mission of the 
FAO Investment Centre Division visiied the States of Gujarat, Rajasthan, 
Orissa and Madhya Pradesh during November, 2000  to  assist  Government  
of India  in  developing  strategy  for 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2001] 
extending Special Programme for Food Security (SPFS) in the country. The 
SPFS provides a comprehensive framework for the range of activities, 
projects and programmes that are undertaken for the purpose of enhancing 
food security in rainfed areas. The stra tegy for extending SPFS is based on a 
decentralized and participatory approach. 
(b) and (c) The Department of Land Resources in the Ministry of Rural 
Development is implementing three main land development and area 
development Programmes namely, Integrated Wasteland Development 
Programme (IWDP), Drought Prone Areas Programmes (DPAP) and Desert 
Development Programme (DDP) through the watershed development 
approach under the Guidelines for Watershed Development w.e.f. 1.4.1995. 
These programmes aim at increasing the soil and moisture conservation and 
productivity of wastelands / degraded lands in the watershed thereby 
increasing income of the people livin g in these areas. They are being 
implemented through community participation following the watershed 
approach. The participation of the local community in planning, 
implementation, monitoring and training for the management of watersheds 
has been recognised as a critical input in these programmes. The project 
activities of the watershed development projects under these programmes as 
decided by the Watershed Committees and the Watershed Associations of the 
local people living in or around the project areas. DPAP is being 
implemented in 961 Blocks of 180 districts in 16 States of the country and 
DDP in 232 Blocks of 40 districts in 7 States. Watershed Development 
Projects under IWDP are generally sanctioned in non-DPAP and non-DDP 
Blocks. At present 11738 projects under DPAP, 5353 projects under DDP and 
298 projects under IWDP are under implementation in the country.

Bicentenary celebrations of Maharaja Ranjit Singh 
463. SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL : Will the Minister of TOURISM 
AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) in what way the Bicentenary of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's 
coronation whose kingdom was the last to lay arms before the British 
is proposed to be celebrated; and 
(b) whether there are any plans to  establish a permanent memorial 
by way of tribute to Maharaja Ranjit Singh? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) and (b) Bicentenary of coronation of Maharaja Ranjit Singh is 
being celebrated by the State Government of Punjab in collaboration with 
Maharaja Ranjit Singh Trust. Government of India (Department of Culture) 
is processing a proposal for setting up a panorama on Maharaja Ranjit Singh 
at Amritsar in consultation with the Government of Punjab. 
Poor condition of ancient monuments In Maharashtra 
464.   SHRI   SURYABHAN   PATIL   VAHADANE:   Will   the 
Minister of TOURISM AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of ancient monuments 
in Maharashtra State are in a bad condition; 
(b) if  so  whether  any  survey  have  been  conducted  by  the 
Government in this regard; and 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2001] 
(c) if so, what steps have been taken by Government to improve the 
conditions of such monuments? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Monuments are annually in spected and surveyed to ascertain 
their condition. Conservation of centrally protected monuments by 
Archaeological Survey of India is an ongoing process. The maintenance and 
conservation of protected monuments are undertaken as per archaeological 
principles, and specific requirement of the monuments subject to the 
availability of funds. 
Development of tourist triangle in West Bengal 
465. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESH WARI: Will the Minister of 
TOURISM AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to develop Sibpur Botanical 
Garden, Bellur Math and Dakhineswaar Ka li Temple as a tourist triangle in 
the State of West Bengal; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a), No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) Development of tourist/pilgrim centres is primarily undertaken by the 
State Governments/UT Administrations. Department of Tourism, 
Government of India, however, provides financial assistance for tourism 
projects prioritised in consulatation with them every year based on the merit 
of proposals and availability of funds. The list of prioritised projects of West 
Bengal for 2001-2002 does not include any project for development of 
Sibpur Botanical Garden, Bellur Math or Dakhineswar Kali Temple.

United Nations' Conference on Racism and other Forms of 
Intolerance 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir, the United Nations' 
Conference against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and 
related intolerance, will be held in Durban (South Africa) from August 
28 to September 1, 2001. The Government of India has so far 
opposed the inclusion of caste and caste-based discrimination in the 
agenda of the Conference. However, like racism, caste discrimination 
is based on the UN definition of "C olour (varna), descent and ethnos" 
fortified by strict rules of endogamy and social segregation. Casteism 
is not a problem limited to India but exists in all countries of South 
Asia and beyond. India has its own constitutional remedies for the ills 
of casteism. Yet, this does not prevent us from receiving global 
solidarity to address this multinational problem, as we do in the case 
of other global issues like child labour, women, AIDS, ecology, human 
rights, etc. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Government to review its stance 
and allow the issue of casteism and caste-based discrimination to be 
included in the agenda of the UN Conference at Durban, as desired 
and urged by various dalit organizations in this country.

required to earmark 10% of its Budget for the development of the North-
Eastern region. If a Ministry fails to spend the whole amount, the unspent

Planning Commission. Out of this pool, the Planning Commission makes 
sanctions for innovative or import ant projects. The funding can be

whether the unspent calance is being credited to the pool or not.

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nominated): It is difficult to

public, more especially in villages and out-of-the-way towns.

and small towns where bookshops and libraries don't exist. While we

650 million literate people who have to be batered to with reading 
materials. Even in big towns, the bookshops are few and far between.

course. But unless the postal rates are reasonable, the book reading 
habit, which is already not very substantive, is going to suffer heavily.

Turn around Package for Revival of Indian Iron and Steel Company 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, I want to draw the attention of the Government of India to the turn 
around package for the revival of Indian Iron and Steel Company - a 
public sector steel making unit. 
The Indian Iron and Steel Company is one of the oldest steel 
manufacturing units in India. 
The Government of India acquired the shares from its owner 
in the year 1973, and, subsequently, the shares were transferred to the 
Steel Authority of India Limited in the year 1974. 
Since 1977 till date, 13 proposals were made by SAIL and 
Government of India to modernize this company, but, unfortunately, no 
proposal was implemented, due to some reason or the other. The 
IISCO has all the infrastructure facilities and huge assets, in the form 
of 2,000 million tonnes of rich iron ore at Gua and Chiria mines and 70 
million tonnes of coal deposits at Chasnalla, Jitpur and Ramnagore 
collieries. The present turnover of IISCO is more than Rs. 900 crores. 
The company, presently, is under the BIFR, and it is 
understood that the BIFR has given an ultimatum to SAIL/Government 
of India, declaring 31 st July, 2001, as the deadline for submission of 
the revival package for the IISCO. It is  further understood that a turn 
around proposal of Rs. 406 crores has been already given to the 
Government by the MECON, which is  under the consideration of the 
Ministry. This turn around proposa l includes Rs. 250 crores to be 
utilised for the VRS, to reduce the manpower by 5000 numbers. 
Incidentally, no steel plant has ever been able to carry out its 
technology upgradation and modernisation from its own resources, 
and, in every case, it had to be provi ded by the Government of India. 
The matter is of utmost importance, and I urge upon the Government 
of India to approve and forward the turn around project to the BIFR, 
before the deadline set by the BIFR, i.e., 31 M July, and save the unit.  
Thank you, Sir.

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI: Madam Chairperson, thank you 
very much for giving me this opportunity to associate myself with the 
matter which was raised by my fri end, Shri V.V. Raghavan, regarding 
the freeze on sale and repurchase of US-64 and the failure of the 
Government-I should say the alleged failure of the Government-to take 
timely action. I fully share the s entiments that he had expressed and 
the spirit behind it. It is an emotive issue and it is an issue which 
concerns millions of people in this country.   As the Leader of the 
Opposition had stated yesterday, rightly or 
257 

RAJYA SABHA        [25 July, 2001] 
wrongly, there is a perception that t here is some kind of protection or 
support of the Government to this particular scheme. He also 
mentioned about the education of the investors. I am afraid that is true. 
It is very necessary and that is wh y, at the outset, I say that the people 
should be educated about the investments, and the various kinds of 
dangers and other possibilities inherent  in them must be explained to 
the people. It is good that various no n-Governmental organisations are 
doing it and so is the Government. But this process has to be carried 
further. Madam, I don't 4 want to go into too much of statistics or regale 
the House with all kinds of other stories, but I want to go into the core 
issues which lie behind this particular matter and the anxiety and the 
concern that has been caused in this country. As we are aware, this 
Scheme was launched in 1964 after a thorough discussion to which a 
reference was made in the House by my friend, Shri Nilotpal Basu. 
That is why it is necessary for us to remember as to why this kind of 
difficulties have arisen. Madam, as it has already been emphasised 
here -- and I am also underscoring it for my purpose -it was really 
intended to mobilise savings. At that point of time, when the savings 
were low, the planning process and the planning development required 
a much higher proportion of savings in the country. This was intended 
and aimed at the small investors. Th is was the main reason. Even the 
Preamble says, "This Act to provide for the establishment of a 
corporation with a view to encouraging savings and investment and 
participation in the income profits and gains accruing to the corporation 
from the acquisition, holding, manage ment and disposal of securities." 
This was the reason. This was the reason why there was confidence in 
the public about the safety of the capital, about the liquidity of one's 
investment and some kind of assured gain or assured return. Madam, 
in the course of time, particularly between the late 80s and early 90s 
many other mutual funds came up. This Scheme was set up by an Act 
of Parliament, as a public corporation or a public company. Its reach 
and importance has been very much, there since then. But, 
unfortunately, when the process of li beralisation started from 90s, the 
changes that were called for, the precautions that were needed, 
unfortunately remained unheeded. One of the important things which 
happened was that over the past 30 years or more the UTI has been in 
existence. This Scheme was natur ally perceived as one of the best 
Schemes. The common people, the middle class people, the salaried 
people and as was said, widows, etc. all these sections thought that 
that was a unique investment for them. But unfortunately, from 1992-
93 onwards, as I said earlier, many other mutual funds began to come 
258 

[25 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
up. So the kind of single monopoly, the kind of protection, the kind of 
ambience, the kind of environment in which the UTI functioned, did no 
longer exist. Unfortunately, this as pect was not properly looked into 
and attended to. 
The other very important thing is that, somehow or the other, 
imperceptibly, its char acter changed. This was also mentioned in 
different ways by Shri Nilotpal Basu, Shri Kapil Sibal, the Leader of the 
Opposition and by others. It is that, the dominant equity component of 
US-64 continued to increase, somehow or the other, for the past 12 to 
13 years, creating difficulties. Now,  this change of character needed 
another look at that point of time. This, I think, is one of the main 
reasons why we are finding ourselves in difficulties today. But, here, I 
would like to say that I agree with the Leader of the Opposition when 
he said, what has happened as regards the UTI will have wider 
repercussions and will have an impact on the integral financial system; 
and we have to keep this in view. We have to take into view the 
integral economy, the integral financial system. I fully agree with him, 
and that is why we will have to take a much wider view on this. The 
second thing that he suggested wa s that there should be systemic 
changes, systemic reforms, though my friend, Mr. Sibal, has said that 
only system solutions are called for,  that the systemic problem is no 
problem. But Dr. Manmohan Singh very rightly said that system 
reforms should be brought about, while, at the same time, wrong-
doing should be prevented, and what has occurred must be dealt with. 
But, I am afraid, I do not find myself in agreement with him and with 
many of my very distinguished colleagues that the Government did not 
take timely action. I think, whatever action was possible at that point of 
time was taken. I don't want to go into the question whether the letter 
received by the Finance Secretary reached the Finance Minister after

the Chairman of the UTI himself, should have realised that this is an 
important matter, and even if Mr. Sinha was sleeping, I think, he could
